summary: Defines managed objects for managing BGP-4 using network management protocols. It fixes errors introduced when the original MIB was converted to SMIv2 and updates references. It documents deployed implementations in a historical context, notes where the MIB fails to represent BGP fully, and replaces RFC 1269 and RFC 1657.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the named counters and status values that network management tools read to watch BGP-4, the protocol routers use to exchange routes between different organizations. It fixes mistakes in the previous version of that definition and lists the places where the definition does not quite match the protocol.

questions: how to monitor bgp peers with snmp
what are the bgp peer states in snmp
subtitle: The standard SNMP objects for watching BGP-4 peers, their timers and the paths they advertise.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard set of SNMP objects to manage BGP-4 routers. The earlier BGP MIB, RFC 1657, carried errors introduced when it was converted to SMIv2, including broken notifications.
tldr.mechanism: The BGP4-MIB defines a few global scalars, a peer table with state, timers and counters for each BGP peer, and tables of received path attributes, plus notifications for a peer entering the established state or falling back.
tldr.outcome: It fixes the conversion errors, adds compliance information and notes where the MIB cannot fully represent BGP. It obsoletes RFC 1269 and RFC 1657.

today: RFC 4273 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2006. It obsoletes RFC 1269 and RFC 1657, and the text itself says that work was in progress to replace this MIB module with a new one representing the current state of the BGP protocol and its extensions.

sections.title: What the BGP4-MIB Is For
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it describes managed objects used for managing the Border Gateway Protocol Version 4 or lower.

The origin of the memo is RFC 1269, which defined managed objects for BGP Version 3 and was updated to support BGP-4 in RFC 1657. This memo fixes errors introduced when the MIB module was converted to use the SMIv2 language, and updates references to the current SNMP framework documents. The module's own revision history lists the changes from RFC 1657: the definitions of the notifications were fixed to be equivalent to their initial definition in RFC 1269; compliance and conformance information was added; information for the values of bgpPeerNegotiatedVersion, bgp4PathAttrLocalPref, bgp4PathAttrCalcLocalPref, bgp4PathAttrMultiExitDisc and bgp4PathAttrASPathSegement was updated; additional clarification comments were added; places where objects do not fully reflect the protocol were noted as Known Issues; and the description of the bgp4PathAttrAtomicAggregate object was updated.

The memo is intended to document deployed implementations of this MIB module in a historical context, to provide clarifications of some items, and to note errors where the MIB module fails to fully represent the BGP protocol. Work was in progress to replace this MIB module with a new one representing the current state of the BGP protocol and its extensions.

The management framework itself is defined elsewhere: managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, the Management Information Base or MIB, and MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms in the Structure of Management Information, and this memo specifies a MIB module compliant with SMIv2, which is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines the names and meanings of the values a management system reads when it wants to know what a BGP router is doing. It replaces two earlier versions and fixes the mistakes that crept into the second one when it was rewritten in a newer definition language.

sections.title: The Shape of the Module
sections.content:
The objects are used to control and manage a BGP-4 implementation. Apart from a few system-wide scalar objects, the MIB is broken into three tables.

  • The BGP Peer Table contains information about the state and current activity of connections with the BGP peers.
  • The BGP Received Path Attribute Table contains path attributes received from all peers running BGP version 3 or less.
  • The BGP-4 Received Path Attribute Table contains path attributes received from all BGP-4 peers.

The actual attributes used in determining a route are a subset of the received attribute tables after local routing policy has been applied.

The module itself is registered at { mib-2 15 } and carries two global objects. bgpVersion is a vector of the supported BGP protocol version numbers, encoded as a string of bits: the first octet contains bits 0 to 7, the second octet bits 8 to 15, and so on, with the most significant bit referring to the lowest bit number in the octet. If a bit, i, is present and set, then version (i+1) of BGP is supported. bgpLocalAs holds the local autonomous system number. Each table has its own branch of the tree: bgpPeerTable at 3, the received path attribute table at 5, the BGP-4 received path attribute table at 6, the notifications at 0, the deprecated traps at 7 and the conformance statements at 8.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the module is three tables: one row for each BGP neighbour, and two tables of the route information those neighbours have sent. Two standalone values hold the BGP version numbers this router supports and its own autonomous system number.

sections.title: The Peer Table
sections.content:
The BGP Peer Table has one entry per BGP peer, indexed by bgpPeerRemoteAddr. Each entry describes one connection with a peer and holds the following kinds of object.

  • Identity and state. bgpPeerIdentifier is the BGP Identifier of the peer and MUST be 0.0.0.0 unless the peer state is openconfirm or established. bgpPeerState is the BGP peer connection state, with the six values idle(1), connect(2), active(3), opensent(4), openconfirm(5) and established(6). bgpPeerAdminStatus is the desired state of the connection, with the values stop(1) and start(2); a transition from stop to start causes the BGP Manual Start Event, and a transition from start to stop causes the BGP Manual Stop Event. It can be used to restart peer connections, and the RFC warns that write access to this object should be provided only with adequate authentication. bgpPeerNegotiatedVersion is the version of BGP running between the two peers, and MUST be zero unless the state is openconfirm or established.
  • Addresses and ports. bgpPeerLocalAddr and bgpPeerLocalPort give the local end of the connection, bgpPeerRemoteAddr and bgpPeerRemotePort the remote end, and bgpPeerRemoteAs the peer's autonomous system number.
  • Counters. bgpPeerInUpdates and bgpPeerOutUpdates count UPDATE messages, bgpPeerInTotalMessages and bgpPeerOutTotalMessages count all messages, bgpPeerFsmEstablishedTransitions counts the number of times the state machine has entered the established state, and bgpPeerFsmEstablishedTime is how long it has been established. bgpPeerLastError holds the last error code and subcode seen on the session, as two octets.

The RFC also removes the wording that suggested initializing the message counters to zero on a transition to the established state. Implementations that still do this remain compliant, but applications should not assume the counters started at zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row of the peer table describes one neighbour: where the connection is from and to, which protocol version was agreed, the state of the session, how many messages have passed, and when the last error happened. Only one value in the row, the administrator's wish to start or stop the session, can be written; everything else is read-only.

sections.title: The Timers of a Session
sections.content:
Each peer entry also carries the timers the BGP speaker uses, split into a configured value and the value actually in force.

  • bgpPeerHoldTimeConfigured is the hold time the speaker puts in the OPEN message it sends. It must not be less than three seconds if it is not zero, and zero means the hold time is not to be established with the peer. The suggested value is 90 seconds. bgpPeerHoldTime is the value actually in force, calculated by the speaker using the smaller of the configured value and the hold time received in the peer's OPEN message; it must be at least three seconds if it is not zero, and it MUST be zero if the hold timer has not been established or if the configured value is zero.
  • bgpPeerKeepAliveConfigured sets the frequency of KEEPALIVE messages relative to the configured hold time; the suggested value is 30 seconds, and a reasonable maximum would be one third of the configured hold time. A value of zero means no periodical KEEPALIVE messages are sent after the connection is established. bgpPeerKeepAlive is the value in force, calculated so that it keeps the same proportion to the hold time as the configured keepalive does to the configured hold time, and it MUST be zero if the keepalive timer has not been established or the configured value is zero.
  • bgpPeerConnectRetryInterval is the ConnectRetry timer, with a suggested value of 120 seconds.
  • bgpPeerMinASOriginationInterval is the interval before the speaker may originate an update for the same destination, with a suggested value of 15 seconds.
  • bgpPeerMinRouteAdvertisementInterval is the interval between route advertisements to the same destination, with a suggested value of 30 seconds for EBGP connections and 5 seconds for IBGP connections.
  • bgpPeerInUpdateElapsedTime reports the time since the last UPDATE was received from this peer.
sections.plainLanguage: Each session runs on timers. The hold timer says how long a session may be silent before it is torn down, the keepalive timer says how often to send an empty message to prove the session is alive, and other timers rate-limit how often new routes may be sent. The table shows both the value the operator configured and the value actually agreed with the neighbour.

sections.title: The Received Path Attribute Tables
sections.content:
The BGP Received Path Attribute Table holds one entry per path to a network, with the path attributes received from all peers running BGP version 3 or less. The BGP-4 Received Path Attribute Table holds one entry per path to a network, with the path attributes received from all BGP-4 peers, and it is indexed by the address prefix, the prefix length and the peer the information was learned from.

Each BGP-4 entry holds the peer that sent the path, the prefix and its length in bits, the origin, the AS path, the next hop, the multi-exit discriminator, the local preference, the atomic aggregate flag, the aggregator AS number and address, the calculated local preference, a flag for whether this is the best path, and any unknown attribute.

The RFC lists where the MIB cannot fully represent the protocol. For the AS path, a path may be longer than 255 octets, which may leave this object holding a truncated AS path, and BGP confederations result in a type of either 3 or 4. The multi-exit discriminator and the local preference are 32-bit values in the protocol, but this MIB uses a signed range from -1 to 2147483647, so the object cannot represent the full range of the protocol; a value of -1 indicates the absence of the attribute. The atomic aggregate attribute is now a primarily informational attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The two path attribute tables record what each neighbour sent about each destination: the origin, the list of networks the route crossed, the next router to use, and the preferences used to choose between routes. Where the protocol can hold a value the table cannot, the RFC says so, for example a 32-bit preference is stored in a signed field that stops short of the protocol's full range.

sections.title: Notifications When a Peer Changes State
sections.content:
Two notifications report session changes. bgpEstablishedNotification is generated when the BGP finite state machine enters the established state, and bgpBackwardTransNotification is generated when the state machine moves from a higher numbered state to a lower numbered state. Both carry the peer's remote address, the last error seen and the current peer state.

The conversion to SMIv2 in RFC 1657 removed the objects from their OBJECTS clause, which broke them. This RFC restores the semantics of the traps as they were initially defined in RFC 1269, and keeps the old objects bgpEstablished and bgpBackwardTransition under the branch bgpTraps at { bgp 7 } with a status of deprecated, noting that no new objects or notifications may be allocated under that branch.
sections.plainLanguage: A management system can be told when a session comes up and when it falls back to an earlier state. The previous version of this definition broke those alerts during a rewrite, and this RFC restores them and keeps the old names as deprecated.

sections.title: Compliance and Object Groups
sections.content:
The module carries compliance statements that say what an implementation has to provide. The current compliance statement, bgp4MIBCompliance, makes three groups mandatory: the globals group, the peer group and the path attribute group. The notification group is separate, and the compliance statement says that implementation of the BGP notifications is completely optional in this MIB.

Two further compliance statements document the history of the module. bgp4MIBDeprecatedCompliances documents deprecated objects, and its description records that the group containing the TRAP objects was improperly converted from SMIv1 in RFC 1657, and that the proper semantics have been restored with the objects in the notification group. bgp4MIBObsoleteCompliances documents obsolete objects, and its group obsoletes the trap group.
sections.plainLanguage: The module says which parts an implementation must have: the tables are required, the notifications are optional. It also keeps two older statements that record what was deprecated and what was dropped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This MIB relates to a system providing inter-domain routing. As such, improper manipulation of the objects represented by this MIB may result in denial of service to a large number of end-users.

Several management objects have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and should be considered sensitive or vulnerable in most network environments. Support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The RFC names them and the risk of each:

  • bgpPeerAdminStatus: an improper change from start to stop can cause significant disruption of the connectivity to those portions of the Internet reached via the applicable remote BGP peer.
  • bgpPeerConnectRetryInterval: an improper change can cause connections to be disrupted for extremely long time periods when otherwise they would be restored in a relatively short period of time.
  • bgpPeerHoldTimeConfigured and bgpPeerKeepAliveConfigured: misconfiguration can make BGP sessions more fragile and less resilient to denial of service attacks on the inter-domain routing system.
  • bgpPeerMinASOriginationInterval and bgpPeerMinRouteAdvertisementInterval: misconfiguration may adversely affect global Internet convergence of the routes advertised by the speaker, which may result in long-lived routing loops and blackholes for the portions of the Internet that use these routes.

A number of managed objects also contain sensitive information about the operation of a network. A BGP peer's local and remote addresses might be sensitive for ISPs who want to keep interface addresses on routers confidential, to prevent router addresses being used for a denial of service attack or spoofing. It is therefore important in most environments to control read access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt the values of these objects when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control over who on the secure network is allowed to access and read or change the objects in this MIB module. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED; instead it is RECOMMENDED to deploy SNMPv3 and enable cryptographic security. It is then the operator's responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is properly configured to give access only to those users that have legitimate rights to read or change them.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the objects are read-only, and that is deliberate: writing to them can cut a router off from part of the Internet. The objects that can be written need access control, and the whole MIB should be read over SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption, because the addresses and session details it exposes are useful for spoofing attacks.

items.title: bgpPeerAdminStatus
items.text: Stopping a peer can cut off the Internet paths that run through it.

items.title: Hold and keepalive configured
items.text: Misconfiguration makes sessions fragile and less resilient to attacks.

items.text: Misconfiguration can cause long-lived routing loops and blackholes.
